newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: U.N. massacre investigators arrive in Congo.
newsitem.headline: U.N. massacre investigators arrive in Congo.

text.p: United Nations investigators arrived on Friday in the Congolese capital Kinshasa to start probing alleged massacres of Rwandan and other Hutu refugees by President Laurent Kabila's forces and their allies.
The team of six, to be joined by two colleagues later in the day, is an advance party due to be followed by more researchers by early next month.

The mission follows persistent reports of alleged massacres deep in the jungles of what was then Zaire by Kabila's rebel forces, who ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko in May, and their Tutsi allies from Rwanda and Burundi.
"I am expecting good cooperation," Georg Mautner-Markhos of the U.N. human rights organisation told reporters on arrival.

"There is a clear understanding between the secretary-general of the United Nations and President Kabila about the investigations. We have now come here to talk with him and see how they can be carried out in practice."

Kabila's soldiers include ethnic Tutsis, traditional rivals of the Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the genocide of up to a million people from the Tutsi minority whose exiled forces then seized control of the country.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees says 250,000 Hutu refugees who had been living in camps in Zaire for more than two years were still unaccounted for. Some 800,000 went home to Rwanda after Kabila's men overran their camps in the east.
The start of the investigation mission has been clouded by a Washington Post report that Kabila told some local officials to do as little as possible to aid it.
Citing unnamed Western and Congolese sources, it said Kabila and other representatives of his new government gave the warning at a meeting in the town of Bukavu last weekend.

They told officials from Kivu Province, on Congo's eastern border with Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi, "not to direct human rights investigators to any mass grave sites or potential witnesses," the Post said.
The sources said Kabila was under intense pressure from Rwandan and Ugandan security officials to stymie the probe.
Rwandan and Ugandan security units played an important part in Kabila's armed uprising that began in October.

In exchange for help to topple Mobutu, Kabila was forced to give those units a free hand in gunning down thousands of ethnic Hutu refugees who had been living in camps in eastern Zaire for over two years, the sources were quoted as saying.
The United States has refused to accept the reports that Kabila may try to hinder the investigation.

"What we know is quite a bit different and that is that in talks with (U.S.) Ambassador (Bill) Richardson and separately in talks with U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, Mr. Kabila agreed to U.N investigations of reported massacres of refugees," spokesman John Dinger said on Thursday.
"And we expect him to keep his word and we fully expect him to cooperate fully with U.N. investIGation."
